title: Every day the best day
hookLine: write it on your heart that every day is the best day in the year (Society and Solitude)
tomorrow: hitch your wagon to a star

cards: Friday. Payday. The trip in the spring.
The day the project ships, the day the kids are older, the day things finally calm down. A good share of a life can be spent leaning toward some other day, the one where living will properly begin.
In a short essay called Works and Days, from his book Society and Solitude, Emerson says something that sounds like a greeting card until you try to do it. Today, which day is the best one.

teach.b: First, the line: "Write it on your heart that every day is the best day in the year." Not the best of the week. The best in the year.
Every one of them. On its face it sounds impossible. Second, owning a day.

teach.h: HE ONLY IS RICH WHO OWNS THE DAY.
teach.b: In the same essay he says, "He only is rich who owns the day," and that nobody owns a day who lets it be overrun by fret and worry. So the best day isn't the one where everything goes right.
It's the one you actually live in, instead of renting it out to tomorrow's anxieties. Third, his picture of the days.

teach.h: THE DAYS COME VEILED, WITH GIFTS.
teach.b: They come and go like veiled figures, sent from a friendly party far away. They say nothing. And if we don't use the gifts they bring, they carry them away again just as quietly.
That's the edge in his line: a day is the best not because it's pleasant, but because it's the only one holding its gifts out to you right now. Fourth, what it isn't.
It isn't a forced smile on a hard day.

teach.h: EVERY DAY IS THE BEST DAY IN THE YEAR.
teach.b: A day can be grief and still be the one you have. It can be dull and still be carrying something. Emerson's challenge is to stop treating today as a waiting room, before its gifts go back out the door unopened.

how: Readers sometimes copy this line from Emerson's Works and Days onto a card or the first page of a journal, as a daily reminder to live the present day rather than wait for a better one.

games.q: what does “every day the best day” mean?
o: a reminder to save your best effort for a holiday
a promise that each new morning will be happier
Emerson's call to live today, not wait for a later one

games.q: inside Works and Days: tap the pairs.
p: every day is the best day

s: Emerson means you should pretend a bad day is a good one
it isn't a forced smile. today is best because it's the one holding its gifts out.
Emerson pictures the days as veiled figures who say nothing
and if their gifts go unused, they carry them silently away.
the line comes from Emerson's essay Experience
it comes from Works and Days, in Society and Solitude.

games.q: a veiled figure arrives at your door holding something out. it says nothing. you're busy worrying about next week. what happens?
o: it leaves, taking its gift with it.
games.why: in Emerson's picture the days come veiled and silent, and if we don't use their gifts, they carry them away just as quietly.

practice: Let today so far pass in front of you without judging it: waking up, the first light, the first conversation.

Look for one small gift the day has already held out, a kind word, a taste, a moment of quiet, that you might have walked past. Then look ahead to the hours left, and wonder what this day might still be carrying.

wordCard.voice: Every day the best day. Emerson's line from Works and Days: write it on your heart, because today is the day holding its gifts out. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the best day. Not the one circled on the calendar; this one. Until tomorrow.
